item.title: The Methodology Behind Times Voter Trends
item.description:
Times Voter Trends reports are based on individual-level estimates of the likelihood that voters would have supported the Democrat, Republican or a minor-party candidate.

The estimates incorporate poll results from The Times/Siena Poll; voter file data from L2; precinct-level election results collected by The New York Times and the Voting and Elections Science Team; county-level election results from The Associated Press; and U.S. Census Bureau data including the Current Population Survey and the American Community Survey.

The L2 voter file is used as the foundation for a synthetic population of registered voters representing the joint distribution of the self-reported demographic characteristics of registered voters in the United States. The probability that each registrant supported the Democratic, Republican or minor party candidate for president in 2024 or 2020 is based on a model of vote choice in Times/Siena polls, fit as a function of respondent’s self-reported demographics, data on the L2 voter file, and geographic data. The resulting individual-level probabilities are adjusted to match the result by precinct.

The estimates do not report a margin of sampling error because they are not based on a sample of the population. The estimates are derived from multiple models, which are each subject to different kinds of error. The results for small subgroups, states without a Times/Siena pre-election poll and states without reliable data on partisanship, like party registration or primary vote history, should be treated with particular caution.

The first post-election L2 voter file with comprehensive vote history in each state is used as the base frame for a synthetic population of registered voters, which represents the joint distribution of the demographic characteristics of registered voters in the United States.

The synthetic population is built iteratively and probabilistically. For each successive trait, the self-reported demographic characteristic of Times/Siena poll respondents is modeled as a function of voter file traits like party registration and vote history, geographic-level predictors, and the respondent’s self-reported characteristics for any previously modeled trait. These models are used to estimate the probability that each registered voter belongs to a given demographic group; the demographic trait assigned to each registrant is simulated probabilistically.

The demographic characteristics were assigned or modeled in this order:

Gender: The L2 voter file contains a likely gender for voters, usually based either on how voters identified on their voter registration form or the likely gender of their first name. The L2 classification is accurate for 99 percent of respondents in recent Times/Siena polls; it is used without revision.

Age: The L2 voter file contains either a date or year of birth for nearly all voters in most states, based on the information provided by registrants when they submit their voter registration form. When age is provided on the L2 voter file, it is used without modification.

However, the voter file does not have age for a meaningful share of the population in some states, such as Alaska, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. For voters without a date or year of birth on the voter file, the age of the registrant is probabilistically simulated based on a model of self-reported age in Times/Siena polls.

Race: The racial classification available on the L2 voter file is never assigned to the registrant — not even in the seven states where state voter files contain the race provided by registrants on their voter registration form.

Race is probabilistically simulated for all registered voters based on multiple models of self-reported race in prior Times/Siena polls. The polls were joined to the given year’s voter file and reweighted to match the voter file by L2’s modeled race, party, age and interactions thereof, with the original survey weight as the base weight. The adjusted survey weight was used in all subsequent race models.

The first model is a Times/Siena polling-based implementation of Bayesian Improved Surname and Geocoding, which estimates the probability of someone’s race based on their surname and geographic information. In traditional BISG, the surname-derived probability of someone’s race is based on the racial composition of people with their surname in U.S. Census data. In this version, the name-based probability is based on a multinomial logistic regression model with cross-validation of self-reported race in previous Times/Siena polls fit as a function of multiple measures of the racial makeup of the respondent’s name: the 2010 decennial Census surname file and the racial makeup of voters’ first, middle and last names on the L2 voter file in the states where voters can provide their race when they register to vote. The geo-level data is Census tract data from the American Community Survey 5-year of the racial composition of the citizen voting age population.

The second model uses a machine learning algorithm, Gradient Boosting, to model self-reported race among previous Times/Siena poll respondents as a function of the aforementioned BISG-like estimate, voter file characteristics, geographic predictors and simulated self-reported traits like age and gender.

Three different versions of the model are fit for states with different data on race and party: one for states with party on the voter file, one for states without party on the voter file (trained on voters from all states, but without partisanship as a predictor) and one for states where self-reported race is available on the voter file (trained only on the states with race on the voter file, with voter file race as an additional predictor variable).

Education: Self-reported education was modeled for all registered voters using three models of self-reported education in Times/Siena polls: a model of whether the respondent had a college degree; a model of whether college graduates had a postgraduate degree; and a model of whether people without a four-year college degree had attended some college. All three models were trained using a machine learning algorithm, Gradient Boosting, which modeled education as a function of self-reported race, age, gender, census-tract educational attainment, census-tract educational attainment by race, turnout, party and salient socioeconomic variables on the voter file, including home value, education and occupation. Separate models were fit for states with and without party registration.

The models were adjusted to match New York Times estimates for the educational composition of registered voters, based on the Census Current Population Survey and the American Community Survey.

The probability that each registrant supported the Democratic, Republican or minor party candidate for president is based on multiple models of vote choice in pre-election New York Times/Siena polls taken from September to November in 2020 and 2024.

Major party and minor party vote choice were modeled separately. The major party models use a machine learning algorithm, Gradient Boosting, to train a model of vote choice in Times/Siena polls as a function of the following covariates:

Age

Race

Education (four categories and two categories)

Gender

Party registration and partisan primary participation

Region (Northeast, South, West, Midwest)

State, if the respondent is from a state poll

Vote history in the last two general elections

Census tract race and ethnicity

Census tract educational attainment

Census tract educational attainment by race and ethnicity

Precinct-level election results in 2024 (or imputed based on the demographic makeup of the precinct)

Precinct-level ecological inference by race and ethnicity (eipack::bayesei)

Two separate models are fit for states with different voter file data on partisanship. One model is fit for states with party registration or primary vote history. It is trained only on data from states with such data.

A second model is fit for states without partisanship data on the voter file. The model is trained on all survey respondents from all states, but without party registration or partisan primary participation as a predictor.

The minor party model was fit using a logistic regression model, with minor party support modeled as a function of the standard self-reported demographic traits, vote history, party registration, precinct-level election results in 2024, and whether the respondent’s ethnicity is classified as likely to be Arab by L2.

The resulting individual-level probabilities were adjusted in multiple steps to match the actual election result by precinct. First, the probability that a voter would support a minor party candidate was adjusted to match the minor party proportion of the vote. Second, the probability that a voter would support a major party candidate was adjusted to match a candidate’s major party vote share in the precinct. Finally, the probability that a voter would support the Democratic or Republican candidate was calculated by multiplying the adjusted Democratic and Republican share of the major party vote by the adjusted major party vote share of the precinct.

The adjustment is calculated by finding a value on the logit scale that minimizes the difference between the actual result by precinct and the mean of the individual-level probabilities among validated voters.

The racial makeup of the electorate is sensitive to question-wording and whether to use the race and ethnicity provided by registrants in the seven states where the voter registration form asks about race.

Across Times/Siena polls from 2020 to 2026, only 90 percent of Times/Siena respondents’ self-reported race aligns with the race they reported when they registered to vote in Alabama, South Carolina, Louisiana, Florida, Tennessee, North Carolina and Georgia. The number is similar, at 92 percent, among those who provided their cellphone number when they registered to vote, suggesting that the difference is mostly due differences in measurement.

The effect varies considerably by race. Among self-reported white voters to the Times/Siena poll, 96 percent reported the same classification when they registered to vote, compared with 93 percent of Black respondents, 74 percent of Hispanics and only 32 percent of other nonwhite voters.

On net, Times/Siena respondents were less likely to identify as white in response to the survey than when they registered to vote. Overall, 63 percent of Times/Siena respondents from the states where self-reported race is available on the voter file identified as non-Hispanic whites in the survey, compared with 65 percent when they registered to vote.

The difference between the survey and voter file-based measures of a respondent’s self-reported race is at least partly a result of differences in question wording, which varies across state voter registration forms and between those forms and The Times/Siena Poll.

Beginning in early 2024, Times/Siena polls have asked the combined race and ethnicity question planned for the 2030 census, not the traditional two-part race and ethnicity question used in the 2020 census. For the Times Voter Trends, responses to the Times/Siena race question have been recoded to more closely align with the 2020 Census definition by reassigning multiracial Hispanics to Hispanic and Middle Eastern and North African respondents to non-Hispanic white. Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, American Indian or Native American, multiracial, and “some other race” have been combined into “other.”

To be classified as “some other race,” respondents had to provide an answer that’s about race, ethnicity or national origin and clearly interpretable to the person responsible for recoding the open-ended answer recorded by the interviewer. For example, “human” is treated as Don’t know/Refused, not “some other race,” and excluded from our modeling because it does not offer a specific race, ethnicity or national origin. Conversely, a respondent recorded as responding “Castanian” is recoded as Don’t know/Refused because the person responsible for coding the race of the respondent doesn’t know whether this is a misheard or misspelled version of Caucasian (White), Kazak (Asian), or something else, not because the respondent themselves doesn’t know or is refusing to answer.

The change in the race and ethnicity question has particularly significant consequences for the composition of the “other” category, making it challenging to compare the 2020 and 2024 results for this group. Consequently, the Times Voter Trends pages do not display the shift between 2020 and 2024 for the “other” race category, as well as the shift between 2020 and 2024 by race in Hawaii, where “other” race represents nearly one-third of the vote.

Source: Times Voter Trends, Current Population Survey, Catalist Voter Behavior Study, Pew Research Center study of validated voters; exit poll conducted by the National Election Pool and Edison Research.

item.title: At Least 12 Injured, Including 6 Minors, in Shooting Near Florida A&M’s Stadium
item.description:
At least 12 people were injured, including six minors, in a shooting near Florida A&M University’s football stadium in Tallahassee, Fla., on Saturday night, shortly after the university’s homecoming game, the police said.

Preliminary findings suggested that an altercation had preceded the shooting, which investigators believed was an isolated incident involving two or three people, the Tallahassee police chief, Lawrence Revell, said at a news conference.

The youngest victim was 11 years old, Chief Revell said. One victim was in critical condition, three were in serious condition and eight were in stable condition. Eleven of the 12 victims had gunshot wounds and one was believed to be a Florida A&M University student, he said.

No suspects were in custody as of Saturday night.

Officers responded just before 8 p.m. to the shooting on two streets near Bragg Memorial Stadium, the police said. Florida A&M University’s football team had faced the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff at the stadium hours earlier.

Florida A&M University is one of the nation’s largest historically Black colleges and universities. Its weeklong homecoming celebration is one of the biggest events on the university’s social calendar, attended by students, faculty and alumni.

Chief Revell said that there were about two dozen officers in the immediate area at the time of the shooting.

item.title: He Took Big Risks to Make Billions. He Wants Georgia Voters to Bet on Him.
item.description:
Rick Jackson, a billionaire entrepreneur with almost no name recognition and even less political experience, called a longtime friend and adviser in February to bring him in on his plans: He wanted to run for governor of Georgia.

Eric Tanenblatt, who had known Mr. Jackson for nearly two decades, was taken aback. The Republican primary race was well underway, and the field was stacked with experienced candidates, including a lieutenant governor with President Trump’s support. Mr. Jackson had just a few months to close an enormous gap.

Mr. Tanenblatt laughed. Mr. Jackson did not.

Mr. Jackson told him he had already set aside $50 million from his personal fortune, and he was willing to pour in much more. By the end of the conversation, Mr. Tanenblatt was convinced Mr. Jackson was approaching the campaign as he did just about everything else.

“He is all in,” Mr. Tanenblatt said. He closed that gap, becoming the Republican nominee.

A pattern of bold gambits, with hard work and confidence pushing up against long odds, has defined much of Mr. Jackson’s life. That willingness to take risks lifted him from a childhood of poverty and neglect to wealth and influence — a pulled-up-by-his-bootstraps story that has been central to his pitch to voters.

“God has blessed me beyond anything I imagined,” Mr. Jackson said during a televised debate in early October. “I know what it means to struggle. I know what it means to get a second chance.”

The campaign has brought intense new scrutiny to how Mr. Jackson has amassed and maintained his fortune.

He has been dogged by claims that his business had resorted to dubious financial maneuvers to avoid paying tens of millions in taxes, leading to a protracted fight with the Internal Revenue Service that his representatives have characterized as “bullying” by the government.

Allegations about his companies’ business practices and the treatment of workers have also resurfaced. In one lawsuit, an immigrant nurse claimed that one of his companies had threatened to report her to the immigration authorities if she quit before her contract was up. (The company settled without admitting wrongdoing.)

Throughout the race, Mr. Jackson has argued that his money insulates him from outside pressure. “I can’t be bought,” he has said repeatedly on the campaign trail. Yet his opponents contend that he was seeking public office to enrich himself and his businesses, which rely on state and federal money.

“He’s spending millions of dollars trying to hold onto the billions he’s making off the taxpayers of Georgia,” Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democrat in the race and a former Atlanta mayor, said at a campaign stop.

And in an election dominated by voter frustrations with affordability, Mr. Jackson’s opponents have sought to emphasize the distance between his humble origins and his reality now. Ms. Bottoms has repeatedly pointed out the features of his 47,000-square-foot mansion in the Atlanta suburbs, such as its 20 bathrooms.

The campaign declined a request for an interview with Mr. Jackson, but it responded to detailed questions about Mr. Jackson’s business history.

In the primary, Mr. Jackson succeeded in forcing the onetime front-runner, Burt Jones, into an expensive and deeply divisive runoff. Early on, while trying to persuade Republican voters, he pledged to be Mr. Trump’s “favorite governor.”

But in the general election, Mr. Jackson has shifted his focus away from Mr. Trump. He has instead relied on ads, campaign stops and a tightly focused message about his personal story of success and struggle.

He talks frequently about the turbulence of his youth — the absent father, the mother who struggled with alcoholism, bouncing between schools and foster homes. He never graduated college; he said he could not afford it.

But in the decades since, he has stitched together a sprawling portfolio of companies and investments encompassing real estate, a Texas data center and faith-based film productions. At the heart of it is Jackson Healthcare, composed of some 20 different companies that mostly provide some kind of medical staffing and consulting services.

That core business, a private entity, now has about $3 billion in revenues, with roughly 2,500 employees, and it has earned Mr. Jackson a place on Forbes’s list of billionaires.

Mr. Jackson, 72, remains chairman and chief executive, but his son Shane Jackson has been the company’s president for more than a decade and handles the day-to-day operations.

Over the course of his career, the elder Mr. Jackson has made blunders, been shoved out of companies he built and periodically run afoul of regulators.

“I have failed more than any human being you’ll ever meet,” Mr. Jackson said in a 2015 interview with The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. “You’re only seeing the businesses that survived. I think the definition of success is getting up one more time than you fall down.”

He has consistently bounced back, with longtime friends and business associates describing him as shrewd and relentless. Early on, to make up for a lack of formal education, he recruited a business professor from Georgia State University to tutor him.

“Because of where he came from, he had a certain drive,” said Dan Melson, who helped start Mr. Jackson’s recruiting business in the late 1970s and has known him for most of his life. He said that Mr. Jackson’s ambition was not about making money: “He was always looking for ways to help other people.”

Mr. Jackson spotted opportunity in a relatively obscure corner of the health care industry. He made a business by providing a steady supply of doctors, nurses and other health care professionals willing to work in out-of-the-way and often undesirable locations.

He started with a physician recruiting business called Jackson and Coker that sent doctors to rural hospitals and clinics in the South.

Mr. Jackson built a thriving staffing business. But he brought in outside investors to help him expand the company, only to have them oust him in the late 1980s. After the business floundered, he bought the assets out of bankruptcy and rebuilt it. He was also among the first to recognize an urgent need for anesthesiologists at smaller, often rural, hospitals.

Mr. Jackson’s businesses had run-ins with regulators, including the ongoing battles with the I.R.S. over the millions in losses that were claimed in his foray into independent filmmaking.

Two years ago, a business under the Jackson Healthcare umbrella and a physician it placed at a separate company reached a $700,000 settlement with the Justice Department over accusations involving a kickback scheme in which the doctor approved orders for unnecessary medical equipment and lab tests for Medicare patients.

Prosecutors credited the Jackson Healthcare business for cooperating with the investigation.

Another one of Jackson Healthcare’s businesses recently agreed to pay $3 million to settle a lawsuit brought by nurses who had been recruited from other countries to work in American hospitals.

The nurses, according to the complaint, said they had been wooed with promises of “the American dream” but were instead told they would have to pay tens of thousands of dollars in “damages” if they left their jobs before the end of their contracts.

Jackson Healthcare has benefited from state contracts, something Mr. Jackson’s political opponents have tried to link to his generous political donations.

One of the company’s businesses was paid more than $40 million through a no-bid state contract to staff Georgia hospitals that were desperate for doctors and health care workers during the pandemic, according to an investigation by Georgia Health News.

Both Mr. Jackson and state officials strenuously denied any connection between the contracts and his donations.

Garrison Douglas, a spokesman for the Jackson campaign, said the company responded to a public health crisis by mobilizing health care workers before the contract was signed.

“No one else could have done this,” Mr. Douglas said in a statement, “but Rick Jackson stepped up when Georgia needed him most.”

Jackson Healthcare has been awarded another contract, worth up to $2.6 billion, to provide medical staffing for federal immigration detention facilities, records show. There is no indication about the status of the work. The campaign said no services have been provided and no money earned on the contract.

Critics and good governance advocates have warned of a potential minefield of conflicts Mr. Jackson’s financial interests could present if he became governor.

Mr. Jackson has vowed to wind down his business with state government if he wins, wanting to avoid “even the appearance that there’s ethics impropriety.”

He said his businesses would terminate existing contracts with the state if he were elected governor and his company would not sign any new ones while he is in office.

He has also proposed enacting more stringent anti-corruption rules, including adding disclosures for conflicts of interest and outside income and adding penalties for self-dealing.

But his campaign declined to say whether he would place his assets in a blind trust, a measure that some ethics experts suggested.

One area of potential conflicts could come from his prolific history of litigation, which could carry over into his governorship. He is involved in a raft of lawsuits stemming from a failed banking venture. He swooped in and put himself in the middle of the legal fight with the company’s creditors.

But friends and associates say he did not enter politics for financial reward. His run for governor came as part of a larger transition in his life, they say, as he devoted more attention to charity work and advocacy for foster children.

He was motivated, in part, by a desire to make a positive difference grounded in his Christian faith. He was also growing older and becoming more mindful of his legacy.

Mr. Tanenblatt said the subject kept coming up more and more in their conversations, as he contemplated what else there was to achieve beyond material wealth. His question, Mr. Tanenblatt recalled: “How can I move from success to significance?”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: She Killed Her 4-Year-Old Girl. Can She Ever Be Considered Sane?
item.description:
Sixteen years ago, Marci Webber killed her 4-year-old daughter, Maggie, in the midst of a psychotic episode, then cut her own wrists. When Ms. Webber’s eldest daughter, then 18, found them in the bathroom, Ms. Webber told her, “Shhh, don’t wake the baby.”

She has been institutionalized in Illinois ever since, but for over a decade she has argued that she no longer needs inpatient care. In November, a judge will decide whether she can go free.

The particulars of Ms. Webber’s case are different from those of Lindsay Clancy, whose recent trial on charges of killing her three young children resulted in a hung jury. Ms. Clancy is scheduled to have a hearing to determine next steps in her case next month. But Ms. Webber’s case offers a look at what long-term institutionalization and involuntary treatment can mean for someone found not guilty by reason of insanity.

Ms. Clancy’s trial lasted three weeks, during which the jury saw autopsy photos and children’s pajamas, and even took a trip to the crime scene. Defense lawyers argued that she was insane, and persuaded all but one juror that she should be found not guilty. Now the prosecutor must decide whether to put her on trial again.

Ms. Webber’s trial, on the other hand, took one day and had one witness, a forensic psychologist. She chose not to have a jury. A judge in DuPage County, the suburban county outside Chicago where the killing occurred, found her not guilty by reason of insanity.

The result has been years of debate and hearings over the role of medications and whether she is stable enough to live outside of a mental health facility. As Ms. Webber has tried to win her freedom, the court has heard conflicting testimony on Ms. Webber’s diagnosis, treatment, behavior and what she says are attempts to force her to take psychiatric drugs.

Prosecutors say Ms. Webber fails to fully grasp the harm she caused, in part because she blames medications, not mental illness, for Maggie’s death.

Involuntary commitment for those found not guilty by reason of insanity is supposed to be for treatment, not punishment. In Illinois, patients may be committed for no longer than what their prison sentence would have been if found guilty — in Ms. Webber’s case, 100 years. There is no minimum.

In many states, such patients receive periodic assessments to determine if inpatient treatment is still needed. In Illinois, a patient may petition the court for release.

In phone interviews from the state hospital where she is being held in Illinois., Ms. Webber spoke of how acutely she missed Maggie. “She was everything to me,” she said.

Years of imprisonment or institutionalization, she argued, will not prevent more children from dying at the hands of their parents. “These mothers are trying to protect their child from something in their heads.”

Ms. Webber, an Army veteran, began taking an antidepressant in the mid-1990s when she was embroiled in a custody dispute with the father of her eldest daughter. Over the years, she was prescribed a host of other antidepressants and antipsychotics, along with a beta blocker sometimes used to treat acute anxiety.

Millions of Americans use medication to treat mental health disorders, and they are considered both safe and effective. A regimen involving several drugs is not necessarily a red flag — experts said it can be desirable in complex illnesses.

But Ms. Webber’s case raises questions that also arose in the Clancy trial, about whether a shifting regimen of psychiatric drugs can contribute to violence. Psychiatric drugs can have adverse effects, particularly when treatment is initiated, doses are changed, or medications are discontinued. If unaddressed, experts say, these side effects may increase the risk of suicide or violence.

Ms. Webber said she had experienced akathisia, an involuntary and sometimes torturous restlessness.

“What they did for years was add meds, switch meds and just continue on,” Ms. Webber said. ‘Nobody thought to say, ‘You know what? I think she’s allergic to this stuff.’”

Dr. Gerard Sanacora, director of the Yale Depression Research Program, said it can be difficult to tease out whether conditions like psychosis are the result of disorders or the drugs being used to treat them.

“These medications are much more likely to help somebody than hurt somebody, but that doesn’t mean that an individual can’t be harmed,” he said.

Ms. Webber was raising three daughters and attending law school in upstate New York when she became obsessively religious, attending Mass daily and traveling 100 miles to a prayer group on weekends, children in tow. When she spotted a praying mantis at a gas station she “rescued” it, believing it was a sign.

Her older daughters had been named after a sitcom character and a president. She named Maggie after Mary Magdalene.

In the Clancy trial, prosecutors sought to portray the defendant as manipulative and controlling, saying she had meticulously planned her children’s death as she had planned their meals and activities.

Ms. Webber said such evidence proved nothing.

“Planning has nothing to do with whether a person is psychotic and insane,” she said. “You will have things that you’re doing that seem totally normal, but on the inside — unless people ask questions — you’re not normal.”

In 2010, Ms. Webber was increasingly worried for Maggie’s safety, believing that she was the target of sexual predators, and moved the girl to her grandmother’s townhouse in Illinois.

Ms. Webber was convinced that Satanists had rented the surrounding properties, and that she was being followed. She kept a knife under her mattress for protection. She felt evil as a physical sensation on her skin.

On a trip to the grocery store, she remembers asking others, “Is there a pill we can take to end our lives if they capture us?”

“You think you can handle it,” she said, “You think, ‘Oh, it’s going to go away or something.’ Until it’s too late.”

Relatives noticed that something was wrong, but Ms. Webber denied it. She now wishes they had asked more questions. She is no longer in touch with her family and asked that they not be contacted, saying that they had been through enough.

In a recent interview on “60 Minutes,” Patrick Clancy, Ms. Clancy’s former husband, offered a glimpse into what friends and relatives face when trying to respond to a deteriorating mental state. “Mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive,” he said.

Ms. Webber was having nightmares and not sleeping. Her paranoia coalesced into “a firm, fixed, false belief,” and she heard a voice telling her that Maggie needed to be saved, she said. She wishes she had been involuntarily hospitalized.

Instead, on Nov. 3, 2010, Ms. Webber’s teenage daughter entered the bathroom to find her sister’s body and the words “divine mercy” written in blood on the wall. Ms. Webber had turned on an audio recorder to capture angels arriving to take her and Maggie to heaven.

In 2014, after the judge’s not guilty verdict and several years of inpatient treatment, Ms. Webber refused psychiatric drugs. Her psychosis did not return, a judge found. Still, in 2017, he denied her release, saying both Ms. Webber and the state needed to do more to prepare. She attempted suicide.

In 2019, that judge released Ms. Webber with a treatment plan, after expressing concern that the state was not treating her fairly.

She returned to her apartment, but prosecutors appealed the judge’s decision and won. After less than two weeks, she returned to the mental institution.

Ms. Webber says that her institutionalization has gone on too long and is harming her physical and mental health.

In one conversation with Ms. Webber, prolonged screaming could be heard in the background. It was a fellow patient who, Ms. Webber said, was in a wheelchair and calling for help.

“God, I can’t stand living like this. Do you hear this?” she asked. “It is the most untherapeutic place you could ever be in.”

Prosecutors have argued that Ms. Webber remains dangerous, citing the suicide attempt, “aggressive, unruly and hostile behavior” and rule infractions. They say that her symptoms improve when she takes medication and worsen when she stops.

Under Illinois law, the burden is now on Ms. Webber to convince a judge that she is not likely to harm herself or others, or would not benefit from continued inpatient care. Her next hearing is in November.

item.title: An Iowa Republican’s Unusual Connection to the Kochs (and Kansas)
item.description:
If there is one thing that Zach Lahn, the Republican nominee for governor of Iowa, definitely does not want to talk about, it’s his connection to the Koch family.

To hear Mr. Lahn tell it, he is a self-made businessman, a father of seven and a farmer running against powerful corporate interests. He has campaigned on his financial independence, pointing to the $2.5 million he lent himself during the primary.

He rode that cash and a right-leaning brand of prairie populism to the nomination, defeating President Trump’s preferred pick in the primary. Now he is facing Rob Sand, the Democratic state auditor, in a race that Democrats view as one of their best shots to flip a governorship.

But there is a more complicated tale of Mr. Lahn’s rise that is interwoven with the Kochs, one of America’s richest and most influential political dynasties.

The story includes years of work for Koch-funded endeavors, a divorce and a new marriage to a former Koch who had just received a sizable divorce settlement of her own. It involves an expanding investment portfolio — including a million-dollar stake in a manufacturer of high-tech penis rings — accusations of carpetbagging and a private plane that has shuttled back and forth to Kansas with two words emblazoned under the wings: “Iowa First.”

“My wife used to be married into the family,” Mr. Lahn, 40, said at a recent town-hall event in Humboldt, Iowa, when asked by a voter about his connection to the Kochs. “But if anyone understands how those situations go, they’re not exactly wanting to support me. I think that’s quite clear.”

In fact, some of the Kochs did not even know his campaign was coming.

At the town hall, Mr. Lahn downplayed his ties to the Kochs. “I have worked for one group that was funded by them one year — for one year — 10 years ago,” he said.

His connections are deeper.

In 2014, Mr. Lahn was hired to lead the Montana chapter of Americans for Prosperity, the conservative advocacy group in the Kochs’ political network. He held the post for about a year and then served as a fund-raiser for the organization into 2016.

At a Koch-funded education conference, he met a woman named Annie Koch, the wife of Chase Koch, son of the billionaire industrialist Charles Koch, one of the nation’s richest men and leading political financiers.

Soon, Mr. Lahn moved to Kansas, where he co-founded a private school with Annie Koch, called Wonder, that was bankrolled by her and her husband.

In 2017, Mr. Lahn started working for the school, which opened in 2018.

Two years later, the Kochs were divorced, and so were Mr. Lahn and his wife. Mr. Lahn and the future Annie Lahn applied for a marriage license 11 days after his divorce was finalized, in June 2020, court records show.

Mr. Lahn’s financial arrangement with the school was unusual.

From 2017 to 2024, he worked 50 hours per week for Wonder, according to Internal Revenue Service records. The records say he was never paid.

“The school was a passion project, 100 percent,” Mr. Lahn said in an interview with The New York Times, adding that the “school never paid me anything.”

He was, however, being paid at the time. Mr. Lahn was directly billing Annie and Chase Koch through a limited liability company, according to an email and invoices later obtained by The Times. Mr. Lahn sent the Kochs monthly bills for “consulting services.”

In 2019, his monthly billings were $20,883, which would add up to an annual salary approaching $250,000. One internal email refers to his compensation as “salary.”

In an email following the interview, Mr. Lahn’s campaign manager, Paul Cordes, stood by Mr. Lahn’s claim that he was never paid by Wonder. Mr. Cordes said the bills were “related to consulting work that also predates the school.”

Mr. Lahn and Annie have also lent money to the school in recent years; tax records last year showed a balance due of about $4.5 million.

Court filings in Mr. Lahn’s divorce offered little hint of the wealth he would later tap into in his run for governor. In the interview, he said the documents did not require him to list all his assets because he went through a “collaborative divorce.”

Many assets, however, were listed, including $6,401 in a retirement account. He reported about $50,000 in joint savings and checking accounts and another $51,000 in a business account. His $210,000 Iowa farmhouse had a $163,750 mortgage balance.

He listed an annual income of $240,000 on one document and an annual income of $380,000 on a child-support worksheet.

The attorney for Mr. Lahn’s ex-wife declined to comment on his finances.

The Kochs’ divorce records are sealed, but a person with knowledge of the settlement, who was granted anonymity to discuss a private agreement, said that Annie received a sum in the eight-figure range.

In the years since marrying Annie, Mr. Lahn’s investment activity surged, mostly through limited liability companies, public records show.

In 2021, he bought a “ski-in, ski-out” lot at the base of a mountain in Whitefish, Mont., valued at $1.5 million, and he bought and sold a home in the same resort valued at $4.5 million. He and Annie bought and sold a three-bedroom home near their farm. He also bought a 1930s-era movie theater in Belle Plaine, Iowa, for $250,000 in 2023 and roughly 435 acres in surrounding Benton County.

In 2021, one of Mr. Lahn’s limited liability companies bought a $1 million stake in FirmTech Inc., a men’s sexual health company that makes penis rings promising longer erections and more intense orgasms. At one point, the company sought to trademark hats that read, “Make America Firm Again.”

Campaign officials say he resigned his position with the company in 2023.

In the interview with The Times, Mr. Lahn noted that before his second marriage, he purchased a Montana apparel company for $3 million, which he said was “100 percent my own money.”

“There’s been plenty of money that I have made prior to the divorce,” he said, citing work for start-up companies and the purchase of rental property in Montana. His campaign declined to provide any details or documentation.

Mr. Lahn bristled at the suggestion that his wife’s divorce settlement had fueled his business career or contributed to the $2.5 million he lent his campaign.

“Silly question,” he called it.

On a windswept day last November, Mr. Lahn began his campaign at the Belle Plaine farmhouse that was built by his great-great-grandfather in 1900. He was surrounded by the seven children he now shares with his wife, Annie.

(The Lahns each had three children from their previous marriages and have since had one child together.)

The event came as a surprise to Chase Koch.

Mr. Koch learned of Mr. Lahn’s campaign — and the supporting role of his children — only when he saw them in media clips, according to two people close to him, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter.

Mr. Lahn declined to say whether he had alerted Mr. Koch about his children’s role in the campaign kickoff.

“We’ve had good communication on this, but I’m not talking about the kids or the family,” he said, adding, “Our family dealings are our family dealings.”

A representative for Mr. Koch declined to comment, citing the children’s privacy.

Mr. Lahn’s residency has emerged as one of the most fraught issues of the race, with Mr. Sand repeatedly accusing him of being a “Kansas carpetbagger.”

Mr. Lahn has said that he lives full-time in Iowa but that his children split their time between the two states.

Flight records first reported by The Des Moines Register showed Mr. Lahn’s private plane frequently shuttling between the states.

“The airplane goes back and forth to pick up the kids as they split time,” Mr. Lahn, a pilot, said in the interview, adding that he was not always flying the plane with “Iowa First” under the wings.

The Lahns also own a 26-acre Frank Lloyd Wright-inspired estate appraised at $1.8 million — complete with an indoor pool and a private lake — just north of Wichita, Kan.

Mr. Sand has aired a pointed TV ad that calls him an “Iowa public school dad.” Mr. Lahn has repeatedly berated Mr. Sand for what he framed as attacks on his children, who attend school in Kansas.

“I am not going to be intimidated on this,” Mr. Lahn said in a heated exchange during a recent debate, vowing to “defend my children from people who’d like to exploit them like you.”

Mr. Sand responded: “This is not about why you’re in Kansas. This is about the fact that you’re not in Iowa.”

Mr. Lahn voted in Iowa years ago but voted in Kansas in 2018, 2020 and 2022. He re-registered in Iowa in October 2024 — just in time to qualify to run for office in 2026.

Mr. Lahn cast an Iowa ballot in the 2024 general election. But voting records that have not previously been reported show he requested that his ballot be mailed to him — in Kansas.

“All my official mail has gone to my assistant for years,” he explained.

Mr. Lahn has tried to turn the tables on the question of familial wealth.

He has repeatedly invoked Mr. Sand’s wife and her family, who for years have been his major political benefactors.

Mr. Sand is married to Christine Lauridsen, who leads her family’s conglomerate, Lauridsen Group, Inc. She and her family have contributed about $5.8 million to Mr. Sand’s campaign for governor.

“He is a billionaire,” Mr. Lahn claimed in a recent ad. “He doesn’t get what regular folks go through.”

Mr. Sand’s campaign declined to respond to the criticism.

Mr. Lahn’s line of attack has puzzled some political observers who are aware of Mr. Lahn’s connection to the Koch family.

“It seems like the objective is more to muddy the waters,” said Eric Woolson, a Republican consultant in Iowa. “I don’t know that it’s going to resonate with most Iowa voters.”

At the Humboldt town hall, Mr. Lahn dismissed talk of his Koch connections as “conspiratorial” and stressed his opposition to the role played by the family’s multinational conglomerate in the agricultural industry.

“They’re not supporting me in any way, shape or form,” he said. “Not a dollar of inside help, a dollar of outside help. Nothing.”

The Koch super PAC, Americans for Prosperity Action Inc., has spent more than $13.3 million on Iowa’s Senate race this year.

The group has spent nothing for Mr. Lahn.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: In Deep Red Kansas, a Trump Loyalist Fights to Defend a Senate Seat
item.description:
In a restored 1920s train station in North Topeka last week, Senator Roger Marshall, Republican of Kansas, listened as a constituent spoke up to complain about how badly President Trump’s tariffs had hurt his family’s manufacturing company.

Customers were pulling back, Zachary Surritt told Mr. Marshall at a Chamber of Commerce gathering, while costs were rising and employees were struggling to make ends meet.

“Our small businesses can’t sit and wait on a promise for things to happen because we’re feeling the crunch right now,” Mr. Surritt told the senator.

Mr. Marshall begged to differ.

“I think your experience is different than most of the other manufacturing companies that I’ve talked to,” the senator said. “Most of them are expanding and business is great.”

It was an unusual message for a Republican facing an unexpectedly steep re-election challenge as voters grapple with economic anxieties exacerbated by tariffs and the costs of the war with Iran. But then Mr. Marshall, a first-term senator who rode Mr. Trump’s political wave into Congress and has styled himself as an ultra-loyal acolyte of the president’s ever since, has never faced much of a challenge in his solidly conservative state.

It may be one reason his closing pitch leans heavily on discounting his own constituents’ concerns.

“Certainly the cost of gas is an issue,” Mr. Marshall told reporters at another stop in Topeka last week, “but now people are coming home saying, ‘Oh, what’s more important than money?’ There are things more important than money to Kansans.”

Back at the Chamber of Commerce event, Mr. Marshall, a tall, somewhat ungainly 66-year-old, flashed his broad, white-toothed smile as he made a similar argument to Mr. Surritt, defending the tariffs as a necessary tool for bringing manufacturing jobs back to the United States and countering unfair trade practices, particularly by China.

“I’m sorry that it’s impacting you in a negative way,” he said. “I look forward to the tariffs coming off, but other countries have got to treat us fairly.”

The encounter encapsulated how Mr. Marshall, who has spent his political career portraying himself as a champion of the state’s farmers, ranchers and small-business owners, is now grappling with the frustrations of some of those same people — many of them lifelong Republicans.

The challenge has Mr. Marshall fighting to keep a Senate seat Republicans have held continuously for more than a century, an almost unheard-of predicament in Kansas politics.

His struggles extend beyond the economy. A New York Times investigation found that Mr. Marshall, who spent decades practicing as an obstetrician-gynecologist before entering politics, sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills, with some patients arrested after failing to appear in court.

He has denounced the revelations as a politically motivated “hit job.”

A campaign finance watchdog group filed an ethics complaint this week alleging that Mr. Marshall illegally used taxpayer funds to pay campaign staff, as well as for political trips and events. The group, End Citizens United, cited an investigation by the Kansas Reflector that found texts and emails suggesting his Senate staff improperly sought to use taxpayer money to pay for campaign trips.

Mr. Marshall’s campaign finance filings listed no staff salaries as recently as the summer, though a more recent one shows staff being paid in the month of October. Aides from Mr. Marshall’s official Senate office have accompanied him to campaign events, at times acting as spokespeople and helping manage his appearances. Though it is not unusual for congressional aides to take on dual rolls supporting campaigns, members of Congress typically take great pains to ensure that political tasks, trips and functions are not paid for by taxpayers.

In a statement, his campaign said “the narrative that Senator Marshall’s campaign has no paid staff is blatantly false. The team is made up of multiple paid, professional campaign staff.”

Mr. Marshall also faced heavy criticism after a bakery owner complained that she had never received payment for $678 worth of cookies bearing the senator’s name and other sweets that his campaign ordered in 2020. After a brief social media furor, the Marshall campaign paid the vendor $1,300, and the senator said he had “absolutely no idea how this happened.”

He has also faced criticism over property he owned in Florida and questions about how much time he has spent in Kansas.

“You don’t live here!” attendees shouted when the topic came up at a recent debate.

Mr. Marshall has dismissed the criticism about the property, which he says he recently sold, calling it “baloney.” He has insisted he spends most of his time in Washington or Kansas and said the Florida home was meant as a place for his wife to decamp while they were visiting family.

Mr. Marshall and his aides did not respond to repeated requests for interviews from multiple Times reporters. During a recent campaign appearance, an aide briefly prevented a Times reporter from remaining at the event.

Mr. Marshall retains formidable advantages in a state where Republicans have dominated federal elections for generations. Mr. Trump carried Kansas by roughly 16 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans hold a substantial voter-registration advantage.

But his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor who founded one of the nation’s largest congregations, has become unexpectedly competitive. Recent polling shows the race in a statistical dead heat, alarming Republican leaders in Washington and prompting millions of dollars in outside spending.

It has also upended the usual financial advantages of incumbency. Mr. Marshall raised roughly $6.7 million and spent $7.2 million winning his first Senate race in 2020. He is now on pace to match or possibly exceed that to defend his seat, an unusual trajectory for a Republican incumbent in a reliable conservative state.

Privately, many Republicans believe Mr. Marshall grew comfortable in what he assumed was a safe seat and waited too long to prepare for a serious challenge, despite urging from colleagues to mount a more robust effort long before Mr. Hamilton entered the race, according to several people familiar with conversations among party leaders and operatives.

But there were signs more than a year ago that Mr. Marshall could be in trouble. At a town hall meeting in March 2025 in western Kansas, constituents confronted him over tariffs, federal spending cuts and the elimination of government jobs. The senator grew increasingly irritated, accused the audience of being rude and abruptly left the gathering as attendees booed and shouted after him.

His office accused Democratic operatives of sabotaging the event, and Mr. Marshall amplified an unsubstantiated allegation that protesters had been paid to attend. He later acknowledged having no firsthand evidence for the claim.

“It was a complete overreaction,” said Bob Beatty, a political science professor at Washburn University who has studied Kansas politics for decades. “He’s in Oakley, Kansas. This is not Berkeley.”

Mr. Beatty said the episode exposed a growing distance between Mr. Marshall and his constituents, who are more accustomed to figures like former Senator Bob Dole and Senator Jerry Moran making themselves accessible even to those who disagreed with them.

Mr. Marshall has since curtailed traditional public town halls and remains elusive on the campaign trail, opting for more controlled gatherings almost exclusively for supporters, including a bus tour this month that crisscrossed the state.

When he does appear, he offers little in the way of personal connection.

At a bus tour stop on a recent rainy afternoon in Abilene, his wife, Laina Marshall, treated Republican attendees to a warm portrait of Mr. Marshall, recalling him as the ambitious young medical student she met more than four decades ago who had dreams of holding elected office.

He listed roughly 100 goals, she recounted, culminating in a plan to enter politics after his medical career, an aspiration that sprang from a fascination with public service stretching back to age 10, when he had asked to visit Dwight D. Eisenhower’s presidential library for his birthday.

The following morning in Topeka, Mr. Marshall offered no such inspirational backstory, saying only that Republicans had recruited him relentlessly to run for Congress.

“Everyone that would ask me to run, they would try to organize, and my wife would tell them ‘He’s not interested,’” he said. “She’s not happy about it now, but she knows it’s the right thing to do.”

For now, Mr. Marshall’s greatest liability may be what has propelled his political rise: his close alignment with Mr. Trump, whose policies have now alienated some of the state’s most important Republican constituencies.

Agriculture has been central to Mr. Marshall’s political identity since he entered politics criticizing Representative Tim Huelskamp, the Republican he defeated in a primary, for losing his seat on the Agriculture Committee.

But as Trump administration policies have disrupted markets and raised costs, Mr. Marshall has more often defended Mr. Trump than challenged him.

When the president last year proposed increasing beef imports from Argentina to lower grocery prices, the move angered American cattle ranchers. But Mr. Marshall said the impact would be minimal, comparing the amount of Argentine beef entering the country to a single hamburger among thousands of tailgates at a Kansas City Chiefs game.

Americans concerned about high beef prices could simply choose to eat something else, he said.

“You can buy chicken, you can buy pork,” he said during an interview with CBS Mornings.

Earlier this year, the Kansas Livestock Association’s political action committee, which supported Mr. Marshall in 2020, declined to endorse him for re-election over tariffs and remarks Mr. Trump made about beef prices being too high.

On other issues, having the president’s ear has proved beneficial. Mr. Marshall has championed year-round sales of E15 ethanol-blended gasoline, which would expand markets for Kansas corn.

During a speech at the White House over the summer, Mr. Trump said Mr. Marshall frequently called him pleading, “you’ve got to save the ethanol.”

At a rally in Wichita on Monday, Mr. Trump explicitly tied the fate of E15 to Mr. Marshall’s political survival.

“With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent,” Mr. Trump said. “But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him. That’s a big deal for Kansas, actually.”

Mr. Hamilton, who has built his candidacy around faith, moderation and finding common ground, has proved difficult to caricature as too far to the left for the state. He has won endorsements from two of the state’s former Republican governors, Mike Hayden and Bill Graves.

Still, Mr. Marshall has worked to cast him as an extremist.

“My opponent, Adam Hamilton, is the most radical liberal Democrat to ever make it this far in a Senate race,” he told supporters in Russell during a recent campaign stop.

“He’s way too woke for Kansas,” he added.

But those attacks have competed for attention with the series of controversies surrounding the senator, which come as Democrats have made corruption in Washington — and how it is costing ordinary Americans — a defining campaign theme.

Mr. Hamilton and allied groups have blanketed the airwaves throughout the state with ads about the senator’s legal action against former patients. Mr. Marshall’s campaign has responded with advertisements featuring former patients praising him as a caring physician.

For all the signs of vulnerability, there remain plenty of voters who see little reason to abandon their senator.

Sidney Hammond, 78, who attended the Abilene event featuring Mr. Marshall’s wife, said the senator had been a dependable advocate for the state’s agricultural communities.

“I don’t know really why it’s that close, because we’re a rural area and Kansas is fairly strong Republican,” he said. “He seems to care about what’s out here in the Midwest.”

But he noted that the senator could do a better job of letting Kansans know where to find him. Mr. Marshall skipped the Abilene stop of his bus tour, where many voters, including Mr. Hammond, had hoped to greet him.

item.title: Latinos Are Now America’s Most Important Swing Voters
item.description:
In the 1990s, politicians fought for the support of soccer moms. In the 2010s, they competed for votes from white working-class voters. Now it is clear: Latinos are the most important swing voters of the 2020s.

Democrats have made gains with Latinos over the past two years, winning back trust with a crucial group of voters who helped fuel President Trump’s return to the White House in 2024. Latino voters now favor Democrats over Republicans by 30 percentage points, according to the latest New York Times/Siena poll.

Note: Figures are rounded. Margins are calculated using unrounded vote shares.

Sources: Figures from 2016 are averages of estimates from validated voter studies. Figures from 2020 and 2024 are estimates from the Times Voter Trends report. Figures from 2026 are based on responses from 458 Hispanic voters in a nationwide Times/Siena poll conducted Oct. 12 to 19, 2026.

By The New York Times

The shift is a striking reversal after Mr. Trump made significant inroads with Latinos, creating the foundation of a multiracial coalition that many believed could signal a long-term political realignment.

But that swing now appears limited and potentially fleeting.

While Democrats have not yet reached the level of support among Hispanic voters they had a decade ago, they have made important gains that could help them win control of Congress.

Hispanic voters make up at least 20 percent of registered voters in nearly two dozen highly competitive House races in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Pennsylvania and Texas, as well as other states. Latino voters could also prove decisive in several Senate races, including in Texas, where Republicans made historic gains in the past two elections. In Iowa and Kansas, traditionally Republican states where Democrats now see a chance to flip Senate seats, Hispanic voters could also play a critical role.

Latino voters have repeatedly shown in polls that neither party has earned their steadfast loyalty.

In the Times/Siena poll, 42 percent said they were dissatisfied with both parties, and 45 percent said they did not see a great deal of difference between the two.

Camilo Cruz, 19, an independent, said he did not trust either political party to improve conditions across the country. “It’s clear that they’re not actually trying to help with things,” he said. “They’re doing the opposite.”

Mr. Cruz, a student in Fort Myers, Fla., works two jobs to make ends meet. “It really doesn’t feel like either party has the best interest of the people in mind,” he said.

For the past two decades, Democrats have had an advantage with Hispanic voters. And many in the party had taken for granted that the growth of the Latino electorate would inevitably hurt Republicans. But in recent years, Democrats’ lead with the group shrank considerably.

In 2024, Mr. Trump had the support of 44 percent of Hispanic voters, according to the Times Voter Trends report, a marked increase from 2016, when 28 percent supported him.

In the latest survey, that support shrank back down to 31 percent.

Republicans gerrymandered several congressional districts in Texas and Florida on the presumption that they would maintain their edge among Hispanic voters. But recent polls suggest the reversal in Latino support could lead to Republican losses in congressional districts Mr. Trump won by double digits.

Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters now say they are supporting Democrats in the midterms — an improvement, though short of the 68 percent that Democrats won in 2016.

The survey suggests Democrats are peeling off a small but significant share of Mr. Trump’s 2024 supporters, with 11 percent of Hispanic Trump voters saying they now plan to support Democrats.

By many measures, Mr. Trump drove both the rise and the fall of Republican support from Hispanic voters. A poll from Equis Research, which focuses on Hispanic voters, found that Mr. Trump’s approval rating had reached a new low among those voters.

“I liked Trump because he was going to make the economy better,” said Janet Fuentes, 34, a political independent living in Chicago who said she voted for Mr. Trump in 2024. “But prices keep going up.”

Much of Democrats’ gains among Latinos have been concentrated among younger voters and people without a college degree — two groups that swung hard toward Mr. Trump just two years ago.

Across every issue polled, Democrats now hold a wide advantage with Hispanic voters, illustrating how Democrats have regained their trust.

The cost of living is the biggest concern for Latino voters, and it is the issue where Democrats hold their widest advantage. By a nearly 30-point margin, more Hispanic voters say they trust Democrats to handle the economy — a striking reversal from two years ago, when Mr. Trump held a slim advantage on the issue.

Note: Figures may not add up to 100 percent because of rounding.

Sources: Fall 2024 New York Times/Siena surveys; Respondents from 458 Hispanic voters in a nationwide New York Times/Siena poll conducted Oct. 12 to 19, 2026

By The New York Times

And there are clear signs of the political impact of President Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement: Nearly 20 percent of Hispanic voters now say immigration is a top concern, up from 6 percent last month.

While Hispanic voters were divided on which party to trust on immigration in 2024, they now give Democrats a 27-point lead on the issue.

“The very inhumane way our current administration goes about immigration enforcement is terrible,” said Victor Torres, 42, an engineer living in Houston. “People are being treated like hardened criminals, when they hadn’t done anything actually wrong while they’re here.”

Mr. Torres, a Democrat, said that immigration was the main issue driving his vote this year, and that he trusted Democrats more to tackle it.

A little over one-quarter of Latino voters said they knew someone who was deported or detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the past two years, according to an NBC News/Telemundo survey. The polling suggests this may have implications for voter turnout. Some 17 percent of Hispanic voters said they or someone close to them were considering not voting in person this year over concerns about ICE.

Still, Latinos are more enthusiastic than white, Black or Asian American voters heading into the midterm elections, according to the Times/Siena poll. Some 30 percent of Latino voters described their feelings as excited, happy or hopeful.

“A lot more people my age — Gen Z — are speaking out and actually voting,” said Paola Paredes, 21, a student and National Guard member living in San Antonio who is registered as an independent. She plans to vote for James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas. “A lot of my friends rushed to register to vote,” she said.

Amid the encouraging news for Democrats, there are signs that they cannot necessarily count on steadfast support from Hispanic voters. While the party has made gains since 2024, that support has not returned to the levels in 2016, when Democrats held a nearly 40-point advantage.

And over the past decade, negative views of the Democratic Party have been on the rise among Latino voters, according to the NBC/Telemundo poll, though they leveled off in recent years. At the same time, negative views of the Republican Party rose sharply after 2024.

Vote shares and victory margins for 2016 are averages of estimates from studies of validated voters by the Pew Research Center, post-election assessments by Catalist and exit polls by the National Election Pool. Vote shares and victory margins for 2020 and 2024 are estimates from the Times Voter Trends report. Vote share and victory margin in 2026 is based on responses from 458 Hispanic voters in a nationwide Times/Siena poll conducted from Oct. 12 to Oct. 19, 2026.

item.title: Berkeley Considers Starting a Public Bank With Taxpayer Dollars
item.description:
It’s not often that Berkeley, Calif., a city famous for its progressive values, borrows an idea from the conservative state of North Dakota.

But Berkeley voters next week will consider a ballot measure that would tax property owners to create a public bank, drawing inspiration from a century-old, state-run bank in North Dakota.

If approved, Berkeley would establish a public bank that could offer low-interest loans for community projects, such as affordable housing, and small businesses, proponents say.

There have been efforts over the past decade to create public banks across the country, including in Philadelphia, New Mexico and Los Angeles, but they have run into regulatory and political hurdles. San Francisco, across the bay from Berkeley, also has a public bank measure on its ballot next week, but it would create only a governance structure rather than raise funds through a tax.

The push for banks owned by state or local governments in the U.S. grew out of the Occupy Movement in the early 2010s, as activists sought ways to keep money away from corporations and reinvest local tax dollars into their own communities. Public banks are fairly common worldwide, particularly in China, India and Germany.

Berkeley proponents say that the city of 122,000 residents should have a locally-controlled bank that is socially minded and avoids investments in fossil fuels and weapons manufacturers.

“It feels like the most powerful institutions and people in the world are becoming more powerful and more wealthy, and are controlling more and more of our lives,” said Will Toaspern, chair of the Coalition to Keep East Bay Money Local, which supports the proposal, called Measure Z. “This is about setting up something that is publicly funded with community leadership that focuses on the things we want.”

Opponents say that they aren’t against the public bank concept, but that Berkeley’s proposal is a high-risk experiment that would misuse public money. Though the bank’s funds would be generated from Berkeley residents, its capital would be available to the entire East Bay region. Opponents say that would unfairly saddle the city with real financial risks.

“This is a bad deal for Berkeley,” said Paul Mathew, a longtime Berkeley resident who is part of Affordable Berkeley, a group opposing the measure.

The proposal will appear on a November ballot in California that is already filled with high-profile tax measures. They include one locally to help rescue Bay Area Rapid Transit and other transportation agencies, as well as statewide proposals to impose a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and make higher taxes on upper-income earners permanent.

Californians have become stingier at the ballot box, as cost-of-living concerns have mounted. In the state’s June election, voters approved a significantly lower share of tax and bond measures than in recent years.

It’s unclear how those trends will play out in Berkeley, one of a handful of progressive California cities that tend to pass ballot measures at higher rates, said Michael Coleman, a municipal tax expert in the state. The city of Berkeley commissioned a poll in April that found 58 percent of likely voters would support the public bank tax, though opinions may have shifted over the past six months.

Berkeley’s measure would institute an annual parcel tax for six years, starting at 6 cents per square foot for homes, and 9 cents per square foot for commercial buildings. Once the fund has collected $40 million, which is expected to take over four years, the city could apply for insurance through the F.D.I.C., as well as certification from the state.

If approved, the bank would not operate like a retail bank but would instead lend money through partner credit unions and community banks. It would not have A.T.M.s or local branches. The measure limits what could be financed to affordable housing, green energy and infrastructure, and small businesses.

In North Dakota, a public bank was created in 1919 after farmers revolted against out-of-state grain cartels and banks that were charging exorbitant interest rates. The state-run bank has helped to extend credit when private banks would not, such as during the Great Recession or natural disasters. It has offered loans to cities for infrastructure improvements that were about one percentage point below market rate, according to the Northeast-Midwest Institute.

“Banking should be a public utility just like water and electricity,” said Walt McRee, president of the nonprofit Public Banking Institute, which advocates public banks nationwide. “The public’s money needs to be in the public’s hands.”

But David Flynn, an economics professor at the University of North Dakota, said it would be difficult to capture the same benefits in Berkeley because the region already has a competitive lending market and the bank wouldn’t have a narrow focus, like North Dakota’s is on the agricultural economy. A public bank, he said, would be less likely to move the needle on lowering housing costs.

“You can’t just pluck it out as if it’s a Lego piece and drop it in Berkeley or San Francisco,” he said.

item.title: Democrats Have Edge Across Four Key House Races in Pennsylvania, Polls Find
item.description:
Democrats trying to unseat Republicans in four battleground Pennsylvania House districts are ahead in two of them, hold a narrow edge in a third and are tied in a fourth, according to new polling from The New York Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University.

The four seats in Pennsylvania are seen as critical examples of some of the fights playing out nationwide. The districts include working-class communities in the state’s northeastern corner, growing towns with large Hispanic populations, a swing Philadelphia suburb and some more conservative parts of the center of the state.

In the 2024 election, Pennsylvania was one of the country’s biggest battlegrounds, and Republicans romped nearly everywhere. President Trump carried the state en route to being re-elected, and it was the only state in the country where Republicans flipped two House seats.

But the new polls show that Democrats are now leading in their bid to flip back both of those districts.

Taken together, the findings in the races for the four seats amount to another warning sign for a Republican Party that is increasingly at risk of losing its narrow House majority.

In Pennsylvania’s Eighth District, Representative Rob Bresnahan, a Republican, trails his Democratic challenger, Paige Cognetti, the Democratic mayor of Scranton, 46 percent to 51 percent. Ms. Cognetti and her supporters have run numerous ads accusing Mr. Bresnahan of profiting from insider stock trading, and voters in Pennsylvania gave her an 11-point edge when asked which candidate they would trust to handle corruption.

In Pennsylvania’s Seventh District, Representative Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican, is behind his Democratic rival, Bob Brooks, the head of a local firefighters union, by five points. In 2024, Mr. Trump won the swing district by three points, and Mr. Mackenzie prevailed by one point.

The survey in the diverse district also found that Mr. Brooks had a wide lead among nonwhite voters, as both candidates court the Hispanic vote in cities such as Allentown.

The other two races are closer.

In Pennsylvania’s 10th District, Representative Scott Perry, a Republican, is tied at 48 percent with Janelle Stelson, a Democrat and former news broadcaster, in a rematch of their 2024 race. Ms. Stelson is favored on the issue that voters said they cared most about — the cost of living — but it has not so far been enough to pull away from Mr. Perry in a district where he is still favored on immigration.

In Pennsylvania’s First District, Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, the Republican, trails his Democratic challenger, Bob Harvie, a local county commissioner in Bucks County, 46 percent to 48 percent. This seat is the mostDemocratic of the four, and Mr. Fitzpatrick is one of only three current House Republicans to represent a district that Mr. Trump lost in 2024.

Money has poured into the race in recent weeks, as Democrats believe this is the year they will finally be able to defeat Mr. Fitzpatrick, who has defied his district’s Democratic lean in presidential elections for a decade.

On the issues, voters repeatedly say they trust Mr. Harvie more. Even on immigration, traditionally an area where Republicans excel, the Democrat has a two-point advantage.

The New York TimesPhiladelphia InquirerSiena University poll

Oct. 16-22

Based on a New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll of 1,607 likely voters across four Pennsylvania congressional districts conducted Oct. 16 to 22. Question wording has been condensed.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

And voters worry that the Republican Mr. Fitzpatrick, whose district has voted against Mr. Trump for president each time Mr. Fitzpatrick has appeared on the ballot, is too cozy with the president. Nearly half of voters said they were worried that Mr. Fitzpatrick was too supportive of Mr. Trump.

Still, Mr. Fitzpatrick is holding his own in the fight for his political life, boosted by the support of 20 percent of voters who say they plan to support Josh Shapiro, the popular Democratic governor who is running for re-election.

All told, across these four congressional races, roughly $100 million in advertising is set to have aired since the start of September, according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact.

Overall, Mr. Trump is unpopular in the districts represented by the four seats, with a 39 percent overall approval rating. Though low, it is higher than his approval rating nationally or statewide in Pennsylvania. Democrats are hoping to take advantage of a favorable political environment.

Mr. Shapiro, who has run well ahead of his Republican challenger, Stacy Garrity, this year, is leading her by 18 points across the four districts, similar to his 19-point margin statewide in a September Times/Inquirer/Siena poll.

But even as Mr. Shapiro is peeling off the support of about 15 percent of Republicans in these districts, those voters appear poised to split their tickets and back G.O.P. candidates in their home communities.

Mr. Perry, who is the former chairman of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, has aggressively defended the war in Iran and backed many of Mr. Trump’s signature policies.

Of the four districts polled, Mr. Trump appears to be the most popular in Mr. Perry’s district. Half of voters there said they approved of the president’s approach on immigration, including 44 percent of political independents.

Voters also seemed to back the Republican Mr. Perry’s support for the president. More said they trusted Mr. Perry to handle immigration and foreign wars, even as Ms. Stelson enjoyed a substantial advantage on cost of living, with more voters saying they would trust her to “do what’s best for ordinary Pennsylvanians.”

Across the four key battlegrounds, economic issues ranked as the most important: 25 percent of voters rated the economy as their top issue, and another 13 percent said that the cost of living or inflation was the most important. No other issue cracked double digits.

Mr. Trump had a 32 percent approval rating when it came to how he was handling the cost of living. Yet the Democratic congressional candidates had only a six-point edge over the Republican incumbents on the issue.

Voter dissatisfaction with Mr. Trump, though, is broadly apparent in the polls.

In the four districts, half of white voters without a college degree — a contingent that is the backbone of Mr. Trump’s base and a decisive voting bloc in Pennsylvania — disapproved of Mr. Trump’s job performance. Sixty percent disapproved of his handling of cost of living.

That dissatisfaction with Mr. Trump’s approach to economic issues among white working-class voters is playing out across the country.

The Democratic candidates in Pennsylvania are not winning among white voters without a college degree. But the 40 percent support they are garnering is a noteworthy incursion into what has typically been the base of the Republican Party during the Trump era.

Overall, Ms. Cognetti had the most favorable image of the eight candidates for the four seats. By a margin of 10 points, more viewed her favorably than unfavorably. That was far better than her opponent, Mr. Bresnahan, who had a net favorability rating of just one point. Particularly concerning for Republicans is his favorability among political independents — a crucial group — with whom he is underwater by 13 points.

Voters also have concerns about Mr. Bresnahan’s character. He is tied for the lowest rating among the eight candidates — 39 percent — when it comes to who voters think has strong character. Ms. Cognetti, on the other hand, tops the list. Half of voters in the Eighth District, including 11 percent of Republicans, said the Democratic Ms. Cognetti had better character than Mr. Bresnahan.

Across all the issues included in the poll, Democrats held one of their widest leads when it came to who voters trusted to address the growing concern about data centers used to power artificial intelligence. In the Seventh District, where data centers have become a central issue, Mr. Brooks had a 10-point advtange over Mr. Mackenzie.

The polls, though, suggest that the issue — despite its prominence in recent television ads — may not be decisive. Just 2 percent of voters listed A.I. or data centers as their top issue.
