item.title: In Texas, Talarico Leans Into Growing Rivalry With Elon Musk
item.description:
A rivalry between the world’s richest person and one of the most prominent Democratic candidates is intensifying during the final stage of this year’s midterm elections.

On the campaign trail in Texas, James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, is increasingly criticizing Elon Musk over his role in the race. Mr. Musk made a huge contribution this fall to a group aligned with Ken Paxton, Mr. Talarico’s Republican opponent, recent campaign finance disclosures showed.

The race in Texas, a pivotal contest that could determine control of the Senate, is now in part a test of whether Democrats can turn Mr. Musk into a political boogeyman and whether his infusion of cash can lift a Republican candidate who has lagged behind his opponent in fund-raising.

“Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars,” Mr. Talarico said at a rally in San Antonio on Saturday, as the crowd booed in disapproval of Mr. Musk. “He wants his very own personal United States senator.”

Representatives for Mr. Musk and Mr. Paxton did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Talarico has stepped up his attacks on Mr. Musk after campaign finance filings revealed earlier this month that Mr. Musk, a Texas resident who has major business interests in the state, donated $158 million to a Republican super PAC that then flipped the same amount to a group allied with Mr. Paxton.

At the University of Texas on Friday, Mr. Talarico said Mr. Musk was trying to “stop the movement that we are building in our state.” The day before that, Mr. Talarico’s campaign released a digital advertisement accusing Mr. Paxton of being beholden to Mr. Musk. “Let’s remind Elon: Texas is not for sale,” says the narrator of the ad.

Mr. Talarico is betting that Mr. Musk’s connection to the contest will hurt Mr. Paxton. It’s not the first time Democrats have made such a wager.

Last year, Mr. Musk and allied groups spent more than $20 million boosting a conservative Wisconsin Supreme Court candidate, who ended up losing to a liberal opponent. Mr. Musk’s efforts, which included campaigning in the state, may have backfired, inflaming Democratic anger as the race increasingly became a referendum on his influence in U.S. government and the slashing of the federal work force that he oversaw.

Other candidates have also tried to channel anger against an onslaught of outside spending to their advantage.

During Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who ultimately won the party’s nomination, repeatedly attacked his rival, Representative Haley Stevens, over the more than $30 million that groups linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee poured into ads boosting her run.

In polls and focus groups in Texas, voters have voiced concerns about corruption and the influence of the wealthy and powerful in politics, said Matt Angle, a Democratic strategist in the state. He argued that Mr. Musk “has made himself the face of” what some voters perceive as the Republican Party’s fealty to megadonors.

At Mr. Talarico’s rally on Saturday, the crowd roared when he brought up Mr. Musk and cheered loudly when he said his own campaign is “funded by 1.3 million individuals who have donated their hard-earned money.”

Mr. Musk has not campaigned with Mr. Paxton. But he has publicly endorsed him and has used his platform on X, the social media company he owns, to attack Mr. Talarico with growing frequency. Mr. Musk posted on X about Mr. Talarico 18 times last week, claiming Mr. Talarico “hates Texas” and disparaging him in other ways.

JT Ennis, a spokesman for Mr. Talarico, said Mr. Musk’s immense spending in the race “isn’t working, so he’s throwing a tantrum.”

For his part, Mr. Paxton speaks about Mr. Musk rarely, if ever, on the trail. But in a recent fund-raising email to supporters, Mr. Paxton praised him.

“Democrats are trying to buy President Trump’s Senate Majority,” Paxton says in the Thursday email, adding, “But Elon Musk REFUSES to let them get away with it.” Mr. Paxton wrote that he was “proud to have Elon’s support at this do-or-die moment in the election.”

Mr. Talarico’s campaign has vastly out-raised Mr. Paxton’s. And for months, Mr. Paxton and his allies had relatively little money to spend on advertisements. But in September, Mr. Trump’s super PAC and a series of groups linked to Mr. Musk and Senate Republicans dumped tens of millions of dollars into outside advertising for Mr. Paxton, hoping to rescue the Republican’s bid to hold the seat for his party.

Mr. Talarico has eschewed corporate PAC money, largely raising small-dollar donations. When criticized for billionaires’ donations to super PACs backing his run, he has responded that outside groups cannot coordinate with campaigns.

At a Paxton rally in Georgetown on Saturday, Republicans had mixed feelings about Mr. Musk’s support. George Gutierrez, 72, who is semiretired and lives in Round Rock, said he was comfortable with the alliance between Mr. Musk and Mr. Paxton.

Bobby Bagwell, 54, expressed discomfort with the idea of the ultrawealthy playing a major role in financing campaigns. But he said it was disingenuous of Mr. Talarico to criticize wealthy donors getting involved in politics when they have given to groups supporting his candidacy.

“I don’t like the idea of a bunch of superrich billionaires throwing their money around,” said Mr. Bagwell, a home-builder who lives in Leander.

Lauren McGaughy contributed reporting from Austin and Georgetown, Texas, and Marisela Cruz contributed reporting from San Antonio.

item.title: Alaska Democrat Postpones Events After ‘Minor Injuries’ in Automobile Collision, Campaign Says
item.description:
Former Representative Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Alaska, a pivotal race, is postponing planned campaign events for Sunday and Monday after sustaining “minor injuries that required medical attention” following an automobile collision on Saturday night, according to her campaign.

The vehicle that Ms. Peltola and her family were in was struck by another driver, Ms. Peltola’s campaign said in a news release. They were en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet in Anchorage, a gathering of the state’s largest organization of Native American tribes.

“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” Cheryl Bruce, Ms. Peltola’s campaign manager, said in a statement.

Ms. Peltola announced a seven-day campaign blitz on Saturday, calling it the “Alaska Always Tour.” On the advice of medical professionals, she is rescheduling events in Fairbanks and Bethel for later in the week, Ms. Bruce said in her statement. The events were previously scheduled to take place on Sunday and Monday. Other events will continue on schedule, the campaign said.

When asked for additional information about the incident, Ms. Peltola’s campaign pointed to the statement from Ms. Bruce and declined to comment further. The authorities did not immediately provide more details about the incident.

Ms. Peltola is challenging Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican seeking a third term, in a race seen as a key battleground in the fight for control of the Senate.

The Alaska race has come under a national spotlight in recent days. The Department of Justice on Thursday asked a federal court to block the certification of the results if Mr. Sullivan loses narrowly, an extraordinary step that President Trump said he ordered.

The Justice Department argued that voters’ confusion over another Republican candidate with the same name as the incumbent — except for a middle initial — could unfairly sway the election. The lawsuit is viewed as highly unlikely to succeed, in part because Alaska’s Supreme Court already ruled that both Mr. Sullivans may remain on the ballot.

Kellen Browning and Evan Gorelick contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump’s Election Attacks Enter New Pre-emptive Phase
item.description:
For months, President Trump has mounted a sustained effort to attack the integrity of U.S. elections while using the federal government to try to assert more control over the voting process overseen by states.

Last week, Mr. Trump opened a new front.

Rather than simply push false claims at his rallies or target voters his administration claims should not be on the rolls, Mr. Trump moved to pre-emptively challenge the certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican candidate narrowly loses.

In doing so, Mr. Trump harnessed the power of the federal government to try to interfere in the voting process before Election Day — essentially trying to nullify an opponent’s potential win before the game has been called.

Even for a president who worked to undermine and overturn the 2020 presidential election, the anticipatory strike reflects a new intensification of Mr. Trump’s attempts to use his official powers to achieve the election results he wants — one that undermines the democratic process, according to election and legal experts. While they say the administration’s lawsuit is unlikely to be successful, the tactic could still further Mr. Trump’s goals by shaking the confidence of voters in the outcome of the race.

“This is part of the election takeover playbook that I’ve seen around the world and unfortunately in some other autocratic environments,” said Michael McNulty, a former senior elections adviser for the U.S. Agency for International Development who has studied election issues around the world, including in El Salvador, Hungary and Venezuela. “Trump has essentially undermined the independence of the D.O.J. and it’s been weaponized.”

The latest phase of Mr. Trump’s strategy centers on the Justice Department, which asked a federal court to block the certification of the election if the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, were to lose by a slim margin. The administration argued the presence of another candidate with a nearly identical name on the ballot has skewed the election toward Democrats.

The issue has already been litigated in the state: In June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired elementary schoolteacher, could appear on the ballot.

But Attorney General Todd Blanche maintained on Sunday that the federal government had a role in inserting itself into the process.

“We’re not saying that the federal government is going to decide who the next senator from Alaska is,” Mr. Blanche said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” He added: “But if it’s clear that there was confusion and that confusion led to an unjust, improper result that is not the will of the Alaskan voters, we want to make sure that the Alaskan system and the Alaskan state courts and the Alaskan electoral process can understand that in a way that lets them do the right thing.”

When asked for comment, the White House referred to an exchange Mr. Trump had with reporters on Saturday about his administration’s efforts to intervene in Alaska, a lawsuit he said was made at his direction. Republicans have asserted that the candidacy of the second Mr. Sullivan is a Democratic scheme to confuse voters. Democrats have said they have no connection to that candidate, who will appear on the ballot without any party affiliation and has said he is running genuine campaign.

“It is a totally corrupt weaponization situation, and they shouldn’t be allowed to do it,” Mr. Trump said of the Democrats in Alaska. “So I recommended it to the D.O.J. They looked at it, they agreed with me, and they’ve gone to court. Let’s see what happens. But that’s pure corruption.”

Election law specialists say Mr. Trump’s lawsuit in Alaska lacks legal basis and will likely fail. But that might not be the point.

The lawsuit is just one piece of a blitz of federal actions by the Trump administration to assert more control over the electoral process that have run into court challenges. Mr. Trump introduced a plan to have the U.S. Postal Service screen mail ballots, only to have it be blocked by the Supreme Court.

The administration has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for refusing to cede to the federal government’s demands to turn over voter rolls. The administration has lost 27 of those cases. The other cases are pending.

Mr. Trump has deployed homeland security investigators to find evidence of illegal voting in states where it has claimed without evidence there is widespread noncitizen voting. A federal judge restricted much of that effort this week.

But with each claim of election fraud, Mr. Trump is creating another platform to sow doubt about the elections and, some state officials and election experts worry, lay the groundwork to challenge the results of the specific contests.

“The goal is obviously not to win the legal case because if so, that would be a complete failure because it’s going to fail,” said Mr. McNulty, senior policy director for Issue One, a nonpartisan group that tracks election issues. “The goal is to create doubt about the process and then use that doubt to justify later intervention or interference.”

Mr. Trump’s frequent attacks on the security of voting machines have raised fears among congressional Democrats and some election officials that he could be setting the stage to contest the results of the November elections.

The lawsuit in Alaska has added a new layer to those worries. The federal challenge could give cover to officials in the state to question the results of the election, experts warned.

The state’s Division of Elections is overseen by Alaska’s lieutenant governor, a Republican, who initially gave the green light to remove the second Mr. Sullivan from the ballot before he was reinstated by the courts. The lieutenant governor, Nancy Dahlstrom, previously challenged Representative Mary S. Peltola, Mr. Sullivan’s primary Democratic opponent in the senate race, for her House seat.

Mr. Trump has installed allies throughout the federal government who have echoed his false claims about voting. And across the country, a number of local election officials who have expressed sympathy with the election-denier movement now occupy key posts.

Benjamin Hovland, who was ousted by Mr. Trump from the independent, bipartisan federal Election Assistance Commission earlier this year, said he worried the various actions by the administration were serving a pretext for lawsuits after Election Day, based on dubious claims of noncitizen voting and fraud in the electoral process.

“What the D.O.J. is tipping its hand to is stepping in as essentially the president’s personal law firm to try to undercut the credibility of election results they don’t like,” Mr. Hovland said. “And that is a pretty horrible prospect.”

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.
